open_obligations: Check that high-confidence errors in Khan et al.'s data are rare enough to address Bowman et al.'s high-stakes concern.
Note the different protocol: two opposing debaters versus one dialog assistant.
Check calibration curves in the high-confidence regime, where Michael et al. report difficulty.
out.other_title: Participants sometimes give confidently wrong judgments and sometimes accept confident-sounding false model claims
out.rationale: Bowman et al. report participants sometimes give confidently wrong judgements and accept confident false model claims in human-model chat. Khan et al. report that in static debate, rejecting human judgements below 75% confidence keeps 65% of questions at 94% accuracy, that debate beats consultancy at all rejection thresholds, and that judges are better calibrated with debate; the protocol and task differ (LLM debate on QuALITY HARD vs chat on MMLU and QuALITY).
out.scope: proposed ADDRESSES: whether high-confidence human judgements are reliable when judges are assisted by debate rather than a single model, on QuALITY HARD

open_obligations: Check calibration specifically in the high-confidence regime, Michael et al.'s problem regime.
Note that Khan et al.'s questions may not include stalemate-inducing complex arguments.
Check whether the 75% threshold was chosen post hoc.
out.other_title: Debate may not extract all knowledge; too-complex arguments could stalemate the judge
out.rationale: Michael et al. hope eliciting judge uncertainty lets debate fail gracefully but find calibration hard at high confidence. Khan et al. report that in static debate rejecting judgements below 75% confidence retains 65% of questions at 94% accuracy, and that judges are better calibrated with debate than consultancy; this does not test the case of arguments too complex for the judge.
out.scope: proposed ADDRESSES: whether judge confidence can make debate fail gracefully, for human judges of LLM debates

text: Human judges give answers as confidences between 5% and 95%, and the paper evaluates classification with rejection: in static debate, rejecting judgements with confidence below 75% retains 65% of questions at 94% judge accuracy. The authors report that across all rejection thresholds debate protocols achieve higher judge accuracy than consultancy protocols, and that human judges are better calibrated with debate than with consultancy.
title: Confident human debate judgements are reliable: 94% accuracy keeping 65% of questions
